title: The messenger in the eastern place
hookLine: Maryam withdraws to a quiet place, and a messenger in the form of a man brings impossible news

lines: A SCREEN, AND THEN A MAN.
I SEEK REFUGE IN THE MERCIFUL.
cards: Maryam is grown now. She withdraws from her family to a place toward the east, the Qur'an says, and puts a screen between herself and them.
Maybe to pray, maybe just to be quiet; the text doesn't say why, and it doesn't need to. Then, in that private place, a man is standing there, where a young woman went so that nobody would be.
Her first words are not a scream. They're a name of God: I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you fear Him at all.

teach.h: OUR SPIRIT, IN THE FORM OF A MAN.
teach.b: The Qur'an tells us who he is before she knows: Allah sent Our Spirit to her, and he took the form of a man, well made.
Muslims understand the Spirit here as the angel Jibril, the same messenger who, as this path will tell later, came to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in a cave.

Notice her first move: she reaches for ar-Rahman, the Most Merciful, the name inside the bismillah, from day one of this path. He answers gently: I am only a messenger of your Lord, to give you a pure son.
Then Maryam asks the most honest question in the story.

teach.h: HOW CAN I HAVE A SON?
teach.b: In Pickthall's translation: “How can I have a son when no mortal hath touched me, neither have I been unchaste?” She doesn't pretend to understand. She asks, and the Qur'an doesn't scold her for it.
The answer is the one Zakariyya heard yesterday, word for word, for his impossible child: Thy Lord saith, “It is easy for Me.” Easy. Not for Maryam; it will be the hardest thing in her life.
Easy for Him. In Surah Al 'Imran the same scene gives the reason: when Allah decides a thing, He only says to it, “Be! and it is.”

teach.h: KUN FA-YAKUN: BE, AND IT IS.

teach.b: Christians know this scene as the Annunciation, and in the Gospel of Luke the angel is Gabriel. Muslims and Christians tell it differently in important ways, and both honor Maryam's courage in that room.
Today the Qur'an gives a young woman alone with a question no human could answer, and an answer that doesn't explain; it just says who is able.

how: Muslims read this scene in Surah Maryam and Surah Al 'Imran and honor Maryam as a woman of faith and purity; the phrase kun fa-yakun is often said when speaking of what only Allah can do.

o: a greeting of peace said when people meet
be, and it is: how Allah brings a thing about
a prayer asking Allah to make something happen

games.q: what's inside the scene — tap the pairs.
p: Jibril, in the form of a man
I seek refuge in the Most Merciful
how can I have a son?

s: the Qur'an scolds Maryam for questioning the angel
she asks how, and the answer comes without rebuke: it is easy for Me (19:21).
Zakariyya and Maryam both hear 'it is easy' about an impossible child
Muslims understand 'Our Spirit' in this scene as the angel Jibril
the same angel who, Muslims say, brought the Qur'an.

games.q: you're Maryam, alone in a quiet place, and a messenger tells you you'll have a son, though no man has touched you. what do you do?
games.why: she asks: how can I have a son when no mortal hath touched me? the answer: thy Lord saith, it is easy for Me (19:20–21).

practice: Let one question come that has no human answer: why this happened, what's next, how something impossible could ever work out. Don't answer it or push it away; ask it honestly, the way Maryam did, and sit next to it.
If you pray, you can hand it to Allah with her words, I seek refuge in the Most Merciful; if you don't, just let the question stay open.

wordCard.voice: Kun fa-yakun, be, and it is: how Allah decides anything, the answer Maryam received to her honest question.

orig.note: Arabic, Qur'an 3:47: be, and it is.

carryVoice: Your line: it is easy for him. Tomorrow, a palm tree in the desert. See you there.
